# Tobit Chapter 2 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Disagreement 1 — TOB 2:1: Feast Name and Register

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "feast of Weeks — which is the holy Pentecost" |
| LOGOS | "feast of Weeks — the holy feast of Pentecost" |
| PNEUMA | "feast of Weeks came around — Pentecost" |

**Issue:** The Greek text uses both the Hebrew calendar designation (heortē pentēkostē, feast of fifty/weeks) and its common Greek name. PNEUMA's casual "came around" undersells the liturgical formality.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS. Both names preserved with appropriate solemnity. "The holy feast of Pentecost" correctly renders the Greek hē hagia pentēkostē.

---

## Disagreement 2 — TOB 2:2: Description of the Invited Guest

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "who remembers the LORD" |
| LOGOS | "who is mindful of the Lord" |
| PNEUMA | "someone who still holds God in his heart" |

**Issue:** The Greek memnēmenon (from mimnēskomai, "to keep in mind/remember") means something more active than mere memory. PNEUMA's expansive paraphrase ("holds God in his heart") adds warmth not in the text. EMET's "LORD" (all caps) introduces an OT divine-name rendering convention inappropriate to the Greek text.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "who is mindful of the Lord" (LOGOS). Best balances faithfulness to the Greek word and natural English.

---

## Disagreement 3 — TOB 2:3: Method of the Dead Man's Death

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "has been strangled and thrown out in the marketplace" |
| LOGOS | "has been strangled and thrown into the marketplace" |
| PNEUMA | "has been murdered and thrown into the marketplace" |

**Issue:** The Greek pepnigmenos is the perfect passive participle of pnigō, "to choke/strangle." It is not a generic murder term. The specific method matters for the story's cultural context — strangulation may indicate a specific form of execution or humiliation.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "has been strangled and thrown into the marketplace" (LOGOS). The specific term must be preserved.

---

## Disagreement 4 — TOB 2:4: Tobit's Immediate Response

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "before I tasted anything I leaped-up and I-took-up him to a room" |
| LOGOS | "Before I had tasted a single bite, I sprang up and carried him to one of the rooms" |
| PNEUMA | "I didn't touch my food. I jumped up right away, carried the body inside" |

**Issue:** "One of the rooms" (eis tina oikēma) is a specific locational detail that PNEUMA generalizes to "inside." The verb ripped (anepēdēsa) means to spring up/leap — both LOGOS ("sprang") and EMET ("leaped") capture this; PNEUMA's "jumped up" is adequate but flat.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS, with "leaped up" substituted for "sprang up" as more energetic. "One of the rooms" preserved.

---

## Disagreement 5 — TOB 2:6: The Amos Quotation

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "Your feasts shall-be-turned into grief and all-your songs into lamentation" |
| LOGOS | "Your feasts shall be turned into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation" |
| PNEUMA | "Your feasts shall be turned to mourning, all your songs to lamentation" |

**Issue:** "Grief" (EMET) vs. "mourning" (LOGOS, PNEUMA) for Greek penthos. In LXX Amos 8:10, penthos = mourning (a state of bereavement expressed publicly), not merely internal grief. LOGOS and PNEUMA agree on "mourning."

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "mourning" (LOGOS/PNEUMA). Penthos specifically denotes ritual/public mourning, not private grief.

---

## Disagreement 6 — TOB 2:8: The Neighbors' Exact Words

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "Still he is not afraid. Already before he has fled on-account-of this" |
| LOGOS | "Has he still not learned his lesson? Once before he had to flee because of this" |
| PNEUMA | "He still hasn't learned his lesson. He had to run for his life once already" |

**Issue:** The Greek eti ou phobeistai has two readings: "he is still not afraid" (EMET literal) vs. the rhetorical function of mocking someone who hasn't been deterred. LOGOS renders the rhetorical question form; PNEUMA renders as a statement.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS. The interrogative form better captures the contemptuous mockery. "Has he still not learned his lesson?" reads as genuine neighbor derision.

---

## Disagreement 7 — TOB 2:9: Sleeping Position

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "I slept beside-the wall of my-courtyard, and my face was-uncovered on-account-of the-heat" |
| LOGOS | "I lay down to sleep against the courtyard wall with my face uncovered because of the heat" |
| PNEUMA | "I lay down near the wall with my face turned up to the sky" |

**Issue:** The Greek has pros to teichos (against/toward the wall) and parakekekalymmenon (uncovered/not veiled). PNEUMA adds "face turned up to the sky" — a natural inference about why the droppings fell into his eyes, but not stated in the text.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS. "With my face uncovered because of the heat" is the text's explanation. PNEUMA's "turned up to the sky" is a reasonable inference but goes beyond the text.

---

## Disagreement 8 — TOB 2:10: The Sparrows and the Blindness

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "their warm-droppings fell into my eyes and produced white-films" |
| LOGOS | "Their droppings fell warm into my eyes and produced white films" |
| PNEUMA | "Their droppings fell into my open eyes while I slept. By morning, white films had formed across both eyes. I was blind." |

**Issue:** PNEUMA adds "while I slept," "by morning," "both eyes," and the summary sentence "I was blind." None of these additions are in the text.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS. "Fell warm into my eyes and produced white films" follows the Greek closely. PNEUMA's additions, though dramatically effective, exceed the text.

---

## Disagreement 9 — TOB 2:11: Anna's Work

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "was working at women's-tasks and was sending [goods] to those-who-hired" |
| LOGOS | "took up women's work and earned wages by weaving" |
| PNEUMA | "took on weaving and needlework — skilled labor, contracted to local employers" |

**Issue:** Erga gynaikeia ("women's work") is a general term in the ancient world for textile production (spinning, weaving, dyeing). LOGOS specifies "weaving" specifically; PNEUMA adds "needlework" and the phrase "contracted to local employers." Both go beyond the Greek.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** EMET structure with LOGOS register: "took up women's work and sent goods to those who had hired her, receiving wages in return." Preserves the specific economic arrangement described in the Greek.

---

## Disagreement 10 — TOB 2:14: Anna's Final Retort

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "And-where are your acts-of-mercy? And-where are your righteous-deeds? See, all-things are-known about-you!" |
| LOGOS | "So where are your acts of mercy now? Where are your righteous deeds? Everyone can see what kind of man you really are!" |
| PNEUMA | "Where's all that mercy of yours now? Where are your famous righteous deeds? The whole world knows what you've become!" |

**Issue:** This is the chapter's climactic line. Three specific issues:
1. PNEUMA's "famous" for eleēmosynai adds a sarcastic edge not quite in the Greek.
2. PNEUMA's "what you've become" implies a change; the Greek idou gnōsta panta peri sou means "behold, all things about you are known" — exposing him, not accusing him of transformation.
3. EMET's "See, all-things are-known about-you!" is the most literal and actually captures the rhetorical power.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** Composite: "So where are your acts of mercy? And where are your righteous deeds? Everything about you is plain for all to see!" — preserves "acts of mercy" (eleēmosynai) exactly as used throughout Tobit, and renders the final phrase with the revelatory force of the Greek.

---

**Total disagreements logged: 10**
